pages.text: Lagoon Side was a crowded settlement of tin roofs and narrow lanes beside a lagoon. Outsiders called it “the Ghetto” and said it was dirty and dangerous. The people who lived there said something else. Mothers fried fish and plantain by the roadside. Fathers repaired motorbikes and mended nets. And in the evenings, the boys played football on a patch of bare ground that they swept clean themselves.

The people who lived there said something else.

Fathers repaired motorbikes and mended nets.
And in the evenings, the boys played football on a patch of bare ground that they swept clean themselves.
pages.alt: A crowded lagoon-side settlement with tin roofs and a patch of ground where boys play football.

pages.text: Awudu, the captain, heard about the Cup: a tournament for community teams from all over the city. “We are going,” he told his friends. “Our boots are broken, and our ball is old, but we have skill and we have heart.” Coach Hubert, a welder who trained them after work, nodded. “Then we will train like champions,” he said. “And play like gentlemen.”

pages.alt: A boy captain and a coach talk to a group of boys holding a battered ball.

pages.text: Madam Matilda, a volunteer teacher, joined the team’s training every Saturday. “Football is wonderful,” she said, “but a good player also reads, writes and counts.” After practice she taught them letters and numbers in the shade of a mango tree. “You will be better footballers if you are also better thinkers,” she said. Caleb, the youngest, raised his hand first every time.

pages.alt: A teacher sits under a mango tree with boys holding notebooks beside a football.

pages.text: On the day of the match, a boy from another team shouted across the pitch, “Ghetto boys cannot play fair! They only know how to steal!” Awudu’s fists tightened. Coach Hubert put a hand on his shoulder. “Show them with your feet and your behaviour,” he said. Awudu took a breath, then nodded. “We will play,” he said. “And we will play fair.”

“And we will play fair.”
pages.alt: A boy clenches his fists as a coach rests a calm hand on his shoulder at a football pitch.

pages.text: At half-time, a stranger in a clean shirt called Awudu aside. “Lose the next half,” he whispered, “and I will give you five hundred cedis for your team.” Awudu’s heart pounded. Five hundred cedis could buy boots, a ball, a lamp for the pitch. “No,” he said. “We play to win or lose honestly.” The stranger shrugged and left. Awudu told Coach Hubert at once.

pages.alt: A boy shakes his head at a man in a clean shirt whispering near the edge of a pitch.

pages.text: In the second half, dark clouds gathered, and rain fell hard. The pitch turned to mud, and the match was stopped. Everyone ran for shelter, because the lagoon’s edge flooded easily. Coach Hubert counted every boy twice. “Nobody goes near the water,” he said. The game restarted the next morning. Lagoon Side lost, one goal to none. Caleb had saved four shots, but the last one slipped in.

pages.text: At the closing ceremony, the organisers announced the winners, and then a surprise: the Fair Play Award. “The team that showed the most honour,” said the chairman, “is Lagoon Side.” The boys erupted in cheers. A coach from a school team shook Caleb’s hand. “Come for a trial next term,” he said. Awudu looked at his teammates, tears of pride in his eyes. “We lost the cup,” he said. “But we kept our name.”

pages.text: Madam Matilda asked the boys to write a summary of the day. Caleb wrote: “A settlement team entered a football cup and met insults and an unfair offer. The captain refused the offer, and the team played honestly through a stormy match. Although they lost by one goal, they won the Fair Play Award, and the goalkeeper was invited for a trial.” Madam Matilda smiled. “That is a good summary,” she said. “It uses your own words and keeps only the main points.”

Caleb wrote: “A settlement team entered a football cup and met insults and an unfair offer.
The captain refused the offer, and the team played honestly through a stormy match.
Although they lost by one goal, they won the Fair Play Award, and the goalkeeper was invited for a trial.” Madam Matilda smiled.
“That is a good summary,” she said.
“It uses your own words and keeps only the main points.”
pages.alt: A boy reads his written summary aloud to a teacher and teammates under a mango tree.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a summary is short, written in your own words, in complete sentences and in the same tense, and it contains only the main points. Caleb left out the weather details and the names. He did not copy sentences from the story. Notice also that he wrote “went” and “refused”, never a chat shortcut. Every community has stories worth summarising. The end.
